name: Rescuing a Project in Crisis
tagline: You take over a running project that is falling apart
scope: A new insurance claims system: migrating data from the old system by a fixed date, a new app for claims adjusters and new hardware at the branches.
intro: Three months ago an insurance company launched a project for a new claims system. The previous project manager has left and the project is now yours. Four sprints remain until the go-live migration – then the old system is switched off and the contract with its vendor ends.
predWorld: Data migration by a fixed date, new branch hardware, the contract with the old system's vendor.
agileWorld: The claims adjusters' app, tuned to how people actually work with it.

stakeholders.name: CEO
stakeholders.quit: lost patience and stopped the project.
stakeholders.epilogBad: called the project an expensive mistake a year later and refused to fund further development.

stakeholders.name: Claims adjusters
stakeholders.wants: an app they can actually work with
stakeholders.quit: refused to use the new system – the project lost its point.
stakeholders.epilogBad: went back to spreadsheets and avoid the new system.

stakeholders.name: IT operations
stakeholders.wants: stability, monitoring and a proper handover
stakeholders.quit: refused to take the system over into operations.
stakeholders.epilogBad: took the system over only on paper – every incident now bounces back to the project team.

takeover.situation: This is the state the project was handed to you in. You have one week to find out what is going on – then you must act.
symptoms: Every app feature has a fixed date in the Gantt chart. Sprint reviews happen, but nothing changes because of them – “the plan is the plan”.
In March the claims adjusters asked to move one field on a form. The monthly board put it on the agenda in May.
Work order is set by whoever pushes hardest – sales on Monday, the CEO on Wednesday, IT on Friday.
The status report for the board of directors has been green for three months. Nobody on the team believes the migration date.
The team works late nights and weekends. Two people have already been on sick leave from exhaustion.
Only Karel understands the data migration. When he was sick for a week, the migration stood still.
takeover.diagLesson: Rescuing a project starts with a diagnosis: from the symptoms (consequences) you trace back to the mechanisms and the form of management causing them. Treating only the symptoms – more overtime, more reports – makes the problem worse.
takeover.lesson: Adding “more management” won't rescue a project. You need to drop the practices that do harm (a detailed Gantt chart for agile work, one board for everything, overtime) and add what is missing: a backlog owner, transparent reporting, knowledge sharing and a plan only for what can be planned.

backlog.name: Handover to operations: documentation and training
Regular training for new branch staff

milestones.name: Migration dress rehearsal
milestones.okText: The trial migration went through and claims adjusters filed the first claims in the new app on migrated data.

milestones.name: Branches ready
milestones.okText: All branches have the new hardware.
milestones.lateText: Some branches are not ready for the migration.

milestones.name: Go-live migration
milestones.okText: The go-live migration is done, the old system is off and claims adjusters work in the new one.
milestones.lateText: The go-live migration only half happened – missing:

gate.title: The board considers stopping the project
gate.text: The board of directors wants to know whether it still makes sense to invest in the project. What do you present?
gate.lesson: When rescuing a project, a true picture of its state is the first step to rebuilding trust. Another “green” report would destroy it for good.

choices.text: The real state, what you changed, and a realistic migration plan
choices.feedback: The board was taken aback but valued the honesty. The project got a chance.

choices.text: A green report as before – surely we'll make it now
choices.feedback: A board member asked about one number and the report fell apart.

choices.text: Ask to postpone the migration by two months
choices.feedback: The delay was approved. But extending the old system costs money.

eventSlots.title: Karel is at the edge
eventSlots.text: After a meeting Karel, the only one who understands the data migration, tells you he can't keep up this pace much longer.
eventSlots.lesson: When a critical part of the project rests on one exhausted person, lighten their load and spread their knowledge – don't motivate them to more overtime.

choices.text: Free Karel from everything but the migration and pair him with Lucie so she learns it
choices.feedback: Karel breathed a sigh of relief. Lucie asks about everything and takes notes.

choices.text: Promise him a bonus if he pulls it off – overtime is necessary now
choices.feedback: Karel nodded. He didn't look thrilled.

choices.text: Hire an external data specialist
choices.feedback: Viktor is expensive, but he understands migrations.

eventSlots.title: The CEO wants a chatbot
eventSlots.text: The CEO saw a chatbot at a competitor and wants one before the migration. “It's just a small feature.”
eventSlots.lesson: Stakeholders have different interests. The PM's job is not to please the strongest one, but to explain the impacts and protect what the project really needs.

choices.text: Explain that the chatbot doesn't belong before the migration and offer it as the first enhancement after
choices.feedback: The CEO frowned but understood. The claims adjusters appreciated someone thinking of them.

choices.text: Add the chatbot right away – the CEO pays
choices.feedback: The CEO is happy. The rest of the project, less so.

choices.text: Build a simple chatbot mock-up for the demo
choices.feedback: The mock-up pleased the CEO and cost two days of work.

eventSlots.title: The trial migration lost data
eventSlots.text: During the trial migration 3 % of insurance claims vanished. Two sprints remain until the go-live migration.
eventSlots.lesson: A data migration error is fixed at its cause (the mapping), not by filling in numbers by hand. Otherwise it comes back in live operations.

choices.text: Stop, find the cause in the data mapping and repeat the trial
choices.feedback: The bug was in converting data from 2009. The second trial passed.

choices.text: Fill in the missing 3 % by hand and move on
choices.feedback: The numbers add up. Why they were missing, nobody knows.

choices.text: Postpone the go-live migration by a sprint
choices.feedback: There's time for the fix. But the CEO is furious.

eventSlots.title: Claims adjusters refuse to test
eventSlots.text: The claims adjusters stopped showing up for testing. “Nobody listens to us anyway.”
eventSlots.lesson: Users nobody listens to stop cooperating. It helps to pull them right into the team and show that their feedback changes things.

choices.text: Invite two claims adjusters into the team for every review
choices.feedback: At the first review an adjuster moved the form field herself. The next day the fix was done.

choices.text: Order testing through the CEO
choices.feedback: The adjusters show up. They stay silent and tick off tests.

choices.text: Hold a one-off workshop
choices.feedback: The workshop was pleasant. Then everything went back to the old ways.

eventSlots.title: IT operations won't take over the system
eventSlots.text: The head of IT operations announces they won't take the system into operations without monitoring and documentation.
eventSlots.lesson: A project ends with a handover. Conditions for the handover to operations belong in the project from the start – otherwise the project team “runs” the system for a year after the end.

choices.text: Agree handover conditions with IT and put them into the plan
choices.feedback: For the first time IT feels like a partner, not an obstacle.

choices.text: Escalate to the CEO to order them
choices.feedback: The CEO ordered it. IT will remember.

choices.text: Promise the project team will support the system on its own for six months
choices.feedback: IT agrees. The team knows what that means for its summer.

eventSlots.title: The old system's vendor
eventSlots.text: The old system's vendor reminds you the contract ends in three weeks. An extension won't come cheap.
eventSlots.lesson: Insurance against a failed migration (the option to go back to the old system) is classic risk management. Refusing it to save money is a gamble.

choices.text: Per the risk register, negotiate a one-month extension as insurance
choices.feedback: The insurance is pricey, but cheaper than claims handling going down.

choices.text: Pay for a three-month extension
choices.feedback: Extended. The budget feels it.

choices.text: Refuse – the migration will make it
choices.feedback: The CEO appreciated the savings.

eventSlots.title: The last week before migration
eventSlots.text: One week to the go-live migration. The CEO suggests the whole team work over the weekend “just to be safe”.
eventSlots.lesson: Before a critical operation you need a rested team and a verified procedure (dress rehearsal, checklist), not exhausted people making mistakes.

choices.text: Dress rehearsal on Friday, weekend off, go-live migration on Monday by the checklist
choices.feedback: The team came in rested on Monday. The checklist caught two forgotten steps.

choices.text: The whole team over the weekend, so we have a buffer
choices.feedback: On Monday morning nobody knew which version of the script was the right one.

choices.text: Half the team on call, half resting
choices.feedback: A compromise. The on-call crew was needed twice.

eventSlots.title: A journalist calls
eventSlots.text: A journalist heard the insurer's project is in trouble and wants a statement.
eventSlots.lesson: Crisis communication rests on short, truthful information through the right channel. Denial comes back to bite.

choices.text: Refer them to the press office with a short, truthful statement
choices.feedback: The article came out short and factual.

choices.text: Say everything is fine
choices.feedback: The journalist had an internal email saying the opposite.

choices.text: No comment
choices.feedback: The article ran under the headline “Insurer Stays Silent”.

karel_odchazi.title: Karel handed in his notice
karel_odchazi.text: Karel is joining a competitor. He wants to spend most of his notice period on vacation.
karel_odchazi.lesson: Paying an exhausted person to do more overtime doesn't work. A knowledge island shows up exactly when time is shortest.
karel_odchazi.unresolvedText: Karel left after the migration and nobody knows why some data look odd.

choices.text: Karel writes up the migration procedure before leaving and Lucie takes it over

team.reason: leaves for a competitor after the handover

choices.feedback: The documentation is brief, but Lucie understands the migration.

choices.text: Talk him into staying until the migration
choices.feedback: Karel stayed. He works, but his mind is elsewhere.

choices.text: Hire an external specialist and let Karel go
choices.feedback: Viktor is learning from the code. Slowly.

chybejici_data.title: Customers are looking for their claims
chybejici_data.text: Customers' open insurance claims have vanished. The call center is swamped.
chybejici_data.lesson: Filling in by hand covered up the bug but didn't remove it. A problem swept under the rug comes back bigger.
chybejici_data.unresolvedText: A year after the migration, lost insurance claims keep turning up.

choices.text: Find the cause, fix the mapping and migrate the affected data again
choices.feedback: Cause found. It hurt, but it's behind us.

choices.text: Handle complaints one by one
choices.feedback: Complaints pile up faster than they get resolved.

choices.text: Set up a team to track them down by hand
choices.feedback: Tracked down. The cause remains.

vypnuti.title: The vendor switches off the old system
vypnuti.text: The contract ended and the vendor switched the old system off. The go-live migration isn't verified yet.
vypnuti.lesson: Without insurance, every migration delay is a crisis. Risk management means preparing a way back before you need it.
vypnuti.unresolvedText: The old system's vendor charged double for the forced extension.

choices.text: Pay for an express extension
choices.feedback: The system is running again. At a price that hurts.

choices.text: Migrate immediately without a dress rehearsal
choices.feedback: The migration happened. What broke along the way remains to be seen.

choices.text: Work on paper without a system for two weeks
choices.feedback: The claims adjusters hauled binders up from the basement.
